questions.question: A student sits in a completely dark room. They turn on a smartphone screen, which lights up, and they can also see a white mug on the table. Which statement correctly describes these objects?
options: Both the smartphone screen and the mug are luminous because they both send light to the student's eyes.
The smartphone screen is luminous because it gives out its own light, whereas the mug is non-luminous because it only reflects light.
The mug is luminous because its white surface generates new light waves when illuminated.
Neither object is luminous because a luminous object must be a natural light source like the Sun.

questions.question: Why can you see your clear reflection in a polished metal sheet but not in a sheet of white paper, even though both surfaces are highly reflective?
options: The paper absorbs almost all of the incident light, while the metal sheet reflects all of it.
The metal sheet reflects light in a regular, single direction, whereas the paper's microscopic roughness scatters the reflected light in many directions.
White paper only reflects white light, whereas polished metal can reflect all individual colors of the spectrum.
The metal sheet acts as a luminous source when light hits it, while the paper remains non-luminous.

questions.question: In a dimly lit room, a person's pupils dilate (get larger). How does this change affect the process of vision?
options: It increases the sensitivity of the retina by physically moving it closer to the pupil.
It allows more light to enter the eye through the pupil to be detected by the light-sensitive retina.
It changes the shape of the pupil so that light rays are scattered before hitting the retina.
It blocks unwanted peripheral light, focusing all light onto the lens instead of the retina.

questions.question: In a theatrical performance, a laser beam is projected across the stage. The audience can only see the pathway of the beam when a fog machine is turned on. Why is this?
options: The fog particles chemically react with the laser light, causing the light to slow down and become visible.
The laser beam only turns into visible light when it is cooled down by the moisture in the fog.
The light from the beam hits the fog particles and scatters towards the audience's eyes, making the path visible.
The fog acts as a transparent medium that lets the light travel in straight lines instead of bending.

questions.question: A person stands 85 meters away from a tall, flat concrete wall and claps their hands. They hear a distinct repeat of the clap a short moment later. What physical process explains this phenomenon?
options: The sound wave is absorbed by the concrete and slowly re-emitted at a lower frequency.
The sound wave reflects off the hard concrete wall and travels back to the person's ears as an echo.
The vibration of the air particles creates a secondary sound wave inside the concrete wall itself.
The sound wave bends around the concrete wall, creating a double sound wave through diffraction.

questions.question: A newly built school hall has very loud, distracting echoes. The school wants to reduce these echoes without using soft, absorbing materials. Which structural change would be most effective?
options: Replacing the flat, smooth wooden walls with highly irregular, textured stone walls to scatter the sound.
Covering the walls with large, highly polished flat metal panels to direct the echoes downwards.
Painting the existing smooth walls with a thick, glossy paint to make them even smoother.
Increasing the height of the flat ceiling while keeping all surfaces perfectly smooth.

questions.question: Why does lining the inside of a noisy machine enclosure with thick, soft foam reduce the noise escaping into the room?
options: The soft foam reflects the sound waves back into the machine with increased frequency.
The foam acts as a vacuum, preventing any particles from vibrating inside it.
Sound waves transfer energy to the soft foam, causing its particles to vibrate and absorb the sound.
The soft foam increases the amplitude of the sound waves until they cancel each other out.

questions.question: A single, narrow beam of light from a torch is directed at a flat pocket mirror. What happens to the direction of the light after it strikes the mirror?
options: It is scattered uniformly in all directions away from the mirror's surface.
It bounces off the mirror and continues travelling in a single, specific direction.
It is split into multiple diverging rays that travel in different directions.
It stops travelling and is completely absorbed at the point of impact.

questions.question: In a physics experiment, a ray of light strikes a flat mirror. The angle between the incoming ray of light and the surface of the mirror is 35 degrees. What is the angle of incidence?
options: 35 degrees, because the angle of incidence is always the angle between the ray and the mirror's surface.
55 degrees, because the angle of incidence is measured between the incoming ray and the normal.
90 degrees, because the normal is always at a right angle to the incident ray.
145 degrees, because it is measured from the opposite flat surface of the mirror.

questions.question: A ray of light is directed at a flat mirror with an angle of incidence of 40 degrees to the normal. Which statement correctly describes the reflected ray?
options: It reflects at 40 degrees to the normal, on the same side of the normal as the incident ray.
It reflects at 50 degrees to the normal, on the opposite side of the normal.
It reflects at 40 degrees to the normal, on the opposite side of the normal.
It reflects at 90 degrees to the normal, travelling along the surface of the mirror.

questions.question: When you look into a flat wall mirror, how is the visual image of yourself formed in your eyes?
options: The mirror acts as a light source, emitting a pre-stored pattern of light directly into your pupils.
Light from you reflects off the mirror obeying the laws of reflection, and some of this reflected light enters your eyes.
Your eyes project light beams onto the mirror, which are then absorbed by the glass to create a picture.
Light is bent around the edges of the mirror, creating a holographic projection in the air in front of you.

questions.question: A toy car is placed 15 cm in front of a flat vertical mirror. If the toy car is then moved 5 cm further away from the mirror, how far will the image of the car appear to be from the actual toy car?
options: 20 cm
30 cm
40 cm
10 cm

questions.question: You stand in front of a flat dressing table mirror and raise your right hand. Which of the following correctly describes the image you see?
options: The image is upside down and appears to raise its left hand.
The image is the right way up and appears to raise its right hand on its own right side.
The image is the right way up but is laterally inverted, appearing to raise its left hand.
The image is rotated 180 degrees horizontally and vertically, raising its right hand.

questions.question: A student places three different sheets of material (glass, cardboard, and tracing paper) one by one between a torch and a wall. Which statement correctly describes how these materials affect the light?
options: Glass is transparent because it transmits light; cardboard is opaque because it does not transmit light.
Cardboard is transparent because it absorbs light; glass is opaque because it reflects all light.
Tracing paper is opaque because it completely blocks all light rays from passing through.
Both glass and cardboard are transparent because they both allow light to travel through them in straight lines.

questions.question: Why does a solid wooden block placed in front of a white screen create a sharp shadow when a single bright lamp is turned on?
options: The wooden block absorbs all the light from the room and re-radiates it as black light onto the screen.
The wooden block blocks the light travelling in straight lines, creating an unlit area on the screen in the shape of the block.
The light rays bend around the corners of the wooden block, leaving only the center of the screen illuminated.
The wooden block chemically reacts with the air to prevent light from reaching the screen behind it.

questions.question: A guitarist plucks a string gently, then plucks the same string much harder without changing where they hold the string on the fretboard. How do the vibrations and the resulting sound change?
options: The frequency of the vibrations increases, making the sound have a much higher pitch.
The amplitude of the vibrations increases, making the sound louder.
The amplitude of the vibrations decreases, making the sound quieter.
The speed of the sound waves increases, making the sound reach the listener faster.

questions.question: A scientist uses an oscilloscope to monitor two sound waves. Wave A has 100 vibrations per second, and Wave B has 400 vibrations per second. What can be concluded about the pitches of these two sounds?
options: Wave B has a higher frequency, which means it has a higher pitch than Wave A.
Wave A has a higher frequency, which means it has a higher pitch than Wave B.
Both waves have the same pitch because frequency does not affect the pitch of a sound.
Wave B has a lower frequency, which means it has a lower pitch than Wave A.

questions.question: Why does sound travel faster through liquid water than through air?
options: Water particles are further apart than air particles, allowing vibrations to jump across gaps faster.
Water particles are much lighter than air particles, so they can vibrate with a higher frequency.
Water particles are closer together than air particles, allowing the vibrations to be passed on more easily.
Water absorbs all sound vibrations, preventing them from spreading out and slowing down.

questions.question: An iron rail and the air next to it are both vibrated by a distant train. A tracker puts their ear to the iron rail and hears the train before hearing it through the air. Why does the sound travel fastest through the solid iron?
options: Solid iron has weak attractive forces between its particles, so they are free to travel quickly along the rail.
The particles in the solid iron have strong attractive forces between them, so many particles vibrate when one does.
The solid iron acts as a vacuum, allowing the sound waves to travel without any particle interference.
The sound waves are converted into light waves inside the solid iron, which travel at a much higher speed.

questions.question: An alarm clock is ringing inside a sealed glass jar. As a vacuum pump removes all the air from the jar, the sound of the alarm fades away until it can no longer be heard, even though the hammer is still seen striking the bell. Why does this happen?
options: The glass jar absorbs more sound when there is no air inside it.
Sound waves are caused by vibrating particles, so they cannot travel through a vacuum where there are no particles.
The vacuum pump reverses the frequency of the sound waves until they become ultrasound.
The lack of air pressure stops the metal hammer from actually vibrating the bell.

questions.question: A student shines a laser beam onto a sheet of white matte paper and a polished metal mirror. Why can the laser spot on the paper be seen from almost any angle in the room, while the spot on the mirror can only be seen from one specific angle?
options: The paper reflects light in a regular way while the mirror scatters light in all directions.
The paper scatters the light in many directions, whereas the mirror reflects the light in a single, regular direction.
The paper absorbs all the light and re-emits it, while the mirror only reflects a small fraction of the light.
The paper is a luminous object that generates its own light, whereas the mirror is a non-luminous object.

questions.question: When a person walks from a brightly lit room into a dark room, their vision takes time to adjust. Which statement correctly describes the pathway of light and the detection mechanism in the eye during this transition?
options: Light enters through the retina, which expands to let more light in, and is detected by the pupil at the front of the eye.
Light enters through the pupil, which becomes smaller to focus light onto the iris at the back of the eye.
Light enters through the pupil, which dilates to let more light in, and is detected by the light-sensitive retina at the back.
Light is emitted by the retina, passes out through the pupil, and reflects back from objects to allow vision.

questions.question: In a clean, dust-free laboratory, a scientist shines a powerful green laser pointer across the room. The laser beam itself is completely invisible until it hits the opposite wall, where a bright green dot appears. Why is the beam invisible in the air?
options: The light in the beam is travelling faster than the speed of light, preventing it from being detected in mid-air.
The light travels in a vacuum within the room, so there are no air particles to absorb the laser energy.
No light from the beam is scattered or reflected towards the scientist's eyes until it hits the wall.
The laser beam is made of non-luminous light that only becomes luminous when it makes contact with a solid surface.

questions.question: An explorer stands in front of a distant, flat cliff face and claps their hands. They hear an echo exactly 1.2 seconds later. Which of the following best explains why this echo occurs?
options: The sound wave is absorbed by the soft cliff face, which slowly vibrates and recreates a new sound wave.
The sound wave reflects off the hard surface of the cliff and travels back to the explorer's ears.
The sound wave travels through the solid cliff, speeds up, and exits the other side to circle back.
The clap causes the air molecules to travel physically to the cliff, bounce off it, and return to the explorer.

questions.question: A recording studio designer wants to prevent echoes in a tracking room without completely deadening the sound. They cover one wall with jagged, uneven wooden blocks of various depths. How does this design help?
options: The irregular wooden blocks absorb all the sound energy, converting it entirely into heat.
The uneven surface reflects sound in a regular, single direction to keep the echo focused away from the microphone.
The irregular surface reflects sound in many different directions, scattering and spreading the sound out to prevent a distinct echo.
The wooden blocks vibrate at a frequency that cancels out the incoming sound waves through destructive interference.

questions.question: Why does lining the inside of a noisy machine enclosure with thick, soft felt significantly reduce the escape of high-pitched squeaks?
options: The felt acts as a vacuum chamber, preventing any particles from vibrating inside the machine.
The sound waves transfer energy to the soft felt by making its flexible particles vibrate, absorbing the sound.
The soft felt has extremely strong bonds between its particles, preventing them from vibrating at all.
The felt reflects the sound waves back and forth so quickly that they speed up and disappear.

questions.question: A highway department is building a barrier next to a residential area to reduce traffic noise. Which combination of materials and strategies would be effective for this purpose?
options: Using a porous, soft material layer facing the highway to absorb the noise, or a solid, hard concrete wall to reflect it away from the houses.
Using a thin, highly flexible plastic sheet that allows the sound waves to pass through without any change in amplitude.
Using a smooth, hard concrete wall to absorb the sound energy, converting it into vibrating mechanical energy inside the houses.
Using an open mesh wire fence that scatters the sound waves into a vacuum.

questions.question: A light ray strikes a flat mirror. The angle between the incoming light ray and the surface of the mirror is 35 degrees. What is the angle of incidence?
options: 35 degrees
55 degrees
90 degrees
70 degrees

questions.question: A ray of light is aimed at a plane mirror such that the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray is 80 degrees. What is the angle of reflection, and where is it measured from?
options: 80 degrees, measured from the mirror's surface.
40 degrees, measured from the mirror's surface.
80 degrees, measured from the normal line.
40 degrees, measured from the normal line.

questions.question: When you look at a glowing candle in a flat glass mirror, you see an image of the candle behind the mirror. Which statement correctly explains why you see this image?
options: The mirror acts as a light source, generating new light rays that match the shape of the candle.
Light from the candle reflects off the mirror obeying the laws of reflection, and some of these reflected rays enter your eyes.
The mirror absorbs the light from the candle and projects a hologram onto the air in front of your eyes.
Light rays pass directly through the silver backing of the mirror and bend toward your eyes from behind the wall.

questions.question: A person stands 2.5 metres in front of a large vertical mirror. They place a small cup on a table 1.0 metre directly behind them. How far is the person's eye from the image of the cup in the mirror?
options: 3.5 metres
5.0 metres
6.0 metres
1.5 metres

questions.question: A student wearing a t-shirt with the word PHYSICS printed on the front stands looking directly into a flat wall mirror. How does the word appear to the student in the mirror?
options: Upside down, but with the letters in the correct left-to-right order.
The right way up, but with the letters reversed horizontally (laterally inverted).
Both upside down and reversed horizontally (laterally inverted).
Exactly the same as it appears on their t-shirt when they look down at it directly.

questions.question: A student tests three sheets of material (X, Y, and Z) by placing them between a light source and a light sensor. Material X lets 98% of the light pass through. Material Y lets 0% of the light pass through. Which classification is correct?
options: Material X is opaque because it transmits light; Material Y is transparent because it blocks light.
Material X is transparent because it transmits light; Material Y is opaque because it does not transmit light.
Material X is transparent because it reflects all light; Material Y is opaque because it refracts all light.
Both materials are transparent because light is a wave that can pass through all matter.

questions.question: When a small, intense light bulb is switched on in the center of a very large, dark hall, which of the following describes how the light travels to the distant corners?
options: The light curves around obstacles at a slow pace, gradually filling the corners of the room.
The light travels in straight lines at an extremely high speed, spreading out in all directions as it moves away from the bulb.
The light travels in spiral paths, maintaining a constant beam width and brightness regardless of the distance.
The light travels in straight lines but slows down continuously until it eventually stops at the boundaries of the hall.

questions.question: A student sets up a point light source, a solid wooden ball, and a white screen. Why does a sharp, dark shadow of the ball appear on the screen?
options: The ball bends the light rays around its surface, focusing them onto a single dark point on the screen.
The ball is an opaque object that blocks the straight-travelling light rays, leaving an unlit area on the screen behind it.
The ball absorbs the light and projects a dark beam of shadow-energy onto the screen.
The light source emits a mixture of light and dark rays, and the ball selectively filters out only the light rays.

questions.question: A musician plucks a guitar string gently, then plucks the same string much harder. How do the vibrations and the resulting sound change when the string is plucked harder?
options: The frequency of the vibration increases, making the sound have a much higher pitch.
The amplitude of the vibration increases, making the sound louder.
The amplitude of the vibration decreases, making the sound quieter but more sustained.
Both the amplitude and frequency decrease, keeping the volume the same but lowering the pitch.

questions.question: A digital sound generator increases the number of vibrations it produces per second from 200 Hz to 800 Hz, while keeping the maximum displacement of the vibrating element the same. What change is heard in the sound?
options: The sound becomes four times louder, but its pitch remains exactly the same.
The sound's pitch becomes higher because the frequency of the vibrations has increased.
The sound's pitch becomes lower because the vibrations occur more slowly.
The sound becomes quieter because high frequencies cannot carry energy as effectively.

questions.question: A referee blows a whistle at the center of a football field. A spectator sitting in the front row hears a very loud sound, while a spectator in the top row of the stadium hears a quiet sound. Why does the sound get quieter further away?
options: The frequency of the sound wave decreases as it travels, which lowers the volume.
The sound wave spreads out as it travels, which decreases the amplitude of the vibrations.
The air particles near the top row are heavier, preventing them from vibrating at all.
The sound wave loses its speed as it travels, causing the vibrations to stop before reaching the top row.

questions.question: Why does sound travel significantly faster through a solid steel rod than through the air?
options: Steel particles are much larger and carry the sound wave physically from one end of the rod to the other.
The steel has no particles inside it, creating a vacuum that allows sound to travel without any resistance.
There are strong attractive forces between the particles in a solid, so when one particle vibrates, many others vibrate almost immediately.
Solids are highly flexible, allowing the sound waves to stretch the particles over long distances very quickly.

questions.question: In a classic physics demonstration, an electric bell is suspended inside a glass jar. As a pump removes the air from the jar, the ringing bell becomes quieter and quieter until it cannot be heard at all. Why does this happen?
options: The vacuum absorbs the sound energy and converts it into light waves inside the jar.
Without air particles to be set vibrating by the bell, the sound wave cannot travel through the vacuum to the outside.
The lack of air pressure stops the bell's hammer from physically striking the metal dome.
Sound waves travel so fast in a vacuum that their frequency becomes too high for the human ear to detect.

questions.question: A student shines a narrow beam of light onto a piece of white paper and a glass mirror. How does the light behave on these two surfaces?
options: The mirror reflects the light in one direction (regular reflection), while the paper does not reflect light at all.
Both surfaces reflect light, but the mirror reflects it in a regular way while the paper scatters it in many directions.
The mirror reflects all the light, whereas the paper absorbs all the light and reflects none.
Both surfaces scatter the light in all directions, but the mirror does so more intensely.

questions.question: An object is placed in a completely sealed, pitch-black room where no light can enter. A person with perfect vision stands in the room. Why can they not see the object?
options: Their eyes need time to adjust to the darkness before they can see the small amount of light emitted by the object.
No light from the object is entering their eyes, which is necessary for anything to be seen.
The human eye can only detect light that has been reflected from a mirror-like surface.
The light from the object is traveling too slowly in the dark to reach their eyes.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the roles of the pupil and the retina when a person looks at a candle flame?
options: Light is emitted from the pupil and is detected when it bounces back onto the retina.
Light enters the eye through the retina and is detected by the light-sensitive pupil at the front.
Light enters the eye through the pupil and is detected by the light-sensitive retina at the back.
Light is focused by the retina and enters the brain directly through the pupil.

questions.question: In a dusty room, a beam of sunlight shining through a window is clearly visible. In a clean room with no dust, the same beam cannot be seen from the side. Why is this?
options: Dust particles block the light, making the area around the beam appear darker and more visible.
The light beam in the clean room travels too fast to be detected by the human eye.
In the dusty room, light hits the dust particles and scatters towards your eyes, making the beam visible.
Dust particles act as miniature light sources that emit their own light when heated by the sun.

questions.question: A person stands in front of a tall, hard stone cliff and shouts. They hear an echo 1.2 seconds later. What caused this echo to occur?
options: The sound wave was absorbed by the cliff and then re-emitted as a new sound wave.
The sound wave reflected off the hard surface of the cliff and travelled back to the person's ears.
The sound wave bent around the cliff and returned from the other side.
The air particles near the cliff vibrated faster, creating a higher-pitched copy of the shout.

questions.question: A recording studio is lined with soft foam panels on the walls. How do these soft panels reduce the sound levels inside the room?
options: The panels reflect all sound waves back to the source, preventing them from spreading.
The panels contain a vacuum which prevents sound waves from travelling through them.
Sound waves transfer energy to the soft panels by making their particles vibrate, absorbing the sound.
The panels increase the frequency of the sound waves until they are too high for humans to hear.

questions.question: A single ray of light travels through the air and strikes a flat, polished silver mirror. What happens to this ray after it hits the mirror?
options: It scatters in all directions because silver is made of tiny irregular crystals.
It is completely absorbed by the silver and converted into thermal energy.
It reflects off the mirror and travels in a single, predictable direction.
It splits into multiple rays that travel parallel to the surface of the mirror.

questions.question: A student is measuring the angles of reflection for a science experiment. From which reference line must they measure the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection?
options: From the surface of the mirror itself.
From an imaginary line drawn at 90 degrees to the mirror's surface, called the normal.
From the line representing the incoming light ray to the outgoing light ray.
From the horizontal table surface on which the mirror is placed.

questions.question: If a ray of light strikes a flat mirror at an angle of 35 degrees to the normal, what will be the angle between the reflected ray and the normal?
options: 35 degrees, on the opposite side of the normal.
55 degrees, on the same side of the normal.
35 degrees, on the same side of the normal.
90 degrees, along the surface of the mirror.

questions.question: When you look at your reflection in a plane mirror, where does the image appear to be located?
options: Exactly on the physical surface of the mirror.
Behind the mirror, at the point where the reflected light rays seem to have come from.
In front of the mirror, halfway between your eyes and the mirror surface.
Inside your eye's pupil, where the rays first cross.

questions.question: A toy car is placed 15 cm in front of a flat vertical mirror. What is the position of the image of the toy car relative to the mirror?
options: 15 cm behind the mirror, directly opposite the toy car.
30 cm behind the mirror, shifted slightly to the left.
7.5 cm behind the mirror, directly opposite the toy car.
15 cm in front of the mirror, superimposed on the toy car itself.

questions.question: You stand in front of a mirror wearing a T-shirt with the word 'PHYSICS' printed on it. How does the word appear to you in the mirror reflection?
options: Upside down and the letters reversed from right to left.
The right way up and exactly the same as you see it on your chest.
The right way up, but laterally inverted (reversed from right to left).
Upside down, but with the letters in the correct left-to-right order.

questions.question: A student holds three sheets of different materials between a lamp and a wall: clear glass, tracing paper, and cardboard. Which statement correctly describes their properties?
options: Clear glass is transparent because it transmits light; cardboard is opaque because it does not transmit light.
Tracing paper is opaque because it reflects all light; cardboard is transparent because it absorbs light.
Clear glass is opaque because it lets light pass; cardboard is transparent because it blocks light.
Tracing paper is transparent because it blocks light; clear glass is opaque because it scatters light.

questions.question: A lighthouse emits a powerful beam of light into the night. Which of the following describes how this light travels through the air?
options: In curved paths at a slow speed, keeping a constant beam width.
In straight lines at an extremely high speed, spreading out as it travels.
In zig-zag patterns at the speed of sound, getting narrower as it travels.
In straight lines at a moderate speed, staying completely parallel without spreading.

questions.question: An opaque circular disc is placed between a small lamp and a white screen. A dark shadow is cast on the screen. What is this shadow?
options: An area where light rays have bent around the disc and met on the screen.
An unlit area in the shape of the disc because the disc blocked the straight-travelling light.
A region where the screen has absorbed the light and re-emitted dark energy.
An area where the light rays from the lamp have been reflected back to the lamp.

questions.question: Two musical notes are played on a piano. The first note is played gently, and the second note is struck very hard, but both keys are the same note (Middle C). How do the sound waves of these two notes compare?
options: The second note has a higher frequency than the first note.
The second note has a greater amplitude than the first note, making it louder.
The first note has a greater amplitude than the second note, making it quieter.
Both notes have the same amplitude, but the second note travels faster through the air.

questions.question: A violinist slides their finger up a string, making the sound go from a low pitch to a very high pitch. What is happening to the physical vibration of the string to cause this change?
options: The amplitude of the vibration is increasing.
The frequency of the vibration is increasing, meaning it vibrates more often per second.
The speed of the sound wave travelling through the air is increasing.
The vibration is stopping completely, leaving only the harmonics.

questions.question: Why does sound travel faster through water (a liquid) than through air (a gas)?
options: Water particles are much lighter than air particles, so they can travel faster from the source to the ear.
Water particles are closer together than air particles, allowing vibrations to be passed on more easily.
Water is a better absorber of sound, which concentrates the energy and speeds it up.
Liquid particles do not vibrate, allowing the sound wave to slide through them without friction.

questions.question: Sound travels through different materials at different speeds. In which of the following materials will sound travel the fastest, and why?
options: Air, because the particles are far apart and have plenty of room to move freely.
Water, because it is a liquid and the particles can easily flow past each other.
Steel, because it is a solid with strong attractive forces between particles so many vibrate when one does.
A vacuum, because there are no particles to block or slow down the sound wave.

questions.question: An astronaut on a spacewalk outside the International Space Station strikes two metal tools together. Why can another astronaut nearby not hear this collision?
options: The space suits completely absorb all internal and external sound vibrations.
Sound is a vibration of particles, and since space is a vacuum with no particles, sound cannot travel.
The temperature in space is too cold for particles to vibrate.
The speed of light in space is too fast, which overrides and cancels out any sound waves.

questions.question: A student shines a laser beam at a sheet of white paper and a glass mirror. Why is the laser beam's spot visible on the paper from many angles, but the beam on the mirror is only visible from one specific angle?
options: The paper absorbs all the light except for a small spot, whereas the mirror reflects all of the light.
The paper has an irregular surface that scatters light in many directions, while the mirror reflects it in a regular, single direction.
The paper acts as a luminous source once illuminated, while the mirror remains non-luminous.
The paper transmits some light which bends its path, while the mirror prevents any transmission.

questions.question: In a completely dark room containing a red apple and a green leaf, a single blue spotlight is turned on, illuminating only the apple. An observer sits in the dark corner of the room. Why can the observer see the apple but not the leaf?
options: The apple emits its own red light in the dark, whereas the leaf requires external light to activate its pigments.
Blue light enters the observer's eyes directly from the spotlight, allowing their brain to construct an image of both objects.
Light from the spotlight reflects off the apple and enters the observer's eye, but no light from any source reflects off the leaf into their eye.
The leaf absorbs all blue light and reflects nothing, while the apple is a luminous object that does not need illumination.

questions.question: In a science fiction film, a spaceship fires a laser beam through the vacuum of outer space. An observer looking from the side sees the beam glowing bright green. Why is this scientifically inaccurate?
options: Laser beams are only visible if they are green, but space vacuums turn all light red.
In a vacuum, there are no particles to scatter or reflect the light beam towards the observer's eye.
Light cannot travel through a vacuum, so the laser beam would stop immediately after leaving the ship.
The vacuum of space completely absorbs light energy, converting it into heat before it can be seen.

questions.question: A person stands 85 meters away from a large, flat concrete wall and claps their hands. They hear a distinct repeat of the clap a short moment later. What physical process explains this second sound?
options: The sound wave was absorbed by the wall and re-emitted at a lower frequency.
The sound wave reflected off the hard concrete surface and travelled back to the person's ears.
The sound wave vibrated the air particles so rapidly that they created a secondary physical clap.
The sound wave refracted through the wall and was amplified by the air on the other side.

questions.question: Why do recording studios cover their walls with bumpy, egg-carton-shaped foam instead of leaving them as flat, painted plasterboard?
options: Bumpy surfaces focus the reflected sound waves into a single, sharp echo towards the microphone.
Irregular surfaces scatter the sound waves in many directions, preventing a strong, distinct echo from returning.
Bumpy surfaces increase the speed of sound, making the recorded audio sound clearer.
Flat surfaces absorb too much sound energy, making the recording room too quiet.

questions.question: When sound waves hit a thick, soft woollen curtain, the sound is significantly muffled. What happens to the energy of the sound waves in this process?
options: The energy is destroyed completely when it hits the dense fibres of the wool.
The energy is converted into light energy as the wool fibres undergo chemical changes.
The sound waves transfer their energy to the soft wool particles, making them vibrate and absorbing the sound.
The sound waves are reflected back and forth inside the curtain until they speed up and escape.

questions.question: A single narrow ray of light from a laser pointer is directed at a highly polished, flat silver mirror. What describes the path of the light after it hits the mirror?
options: It scatters in all directions, creating a diffuse glow across the entire room.
It bounces off the mirror and travels in a single, specific direction as a narrow ray.
It splits into a spectrum of colors, each travelling in a different direction.
It stops completely, depositing all its energy as heat at the point of impact.

questions.question: A student is measuring angles of reflection. They draw a line representing the mirror, and a perpendicular line representing the normal. How should they measure the angle of incidence?
options: From the incoming light ray to the surface of the mirror.
From the outgoing light ray to the surface of the mirror.
From the incoming light ray to the imaginary normal line.
From the normal line to the surface of the mirror.

questions.question: A ray of light hits a flat mirror such that the angle between the incoming ray and the mirror surface is 30 degrees. What is the angle of reflection?
options: 30 degrees
60 degrees
90 degrees
120 degrees

questions.question: When you look at your reflection in a flat bathroom mirror, where does your brain perceive your face to be located?
options: Right on the very front surface of the glass mirror.
Floating in the air halfway between your actual face and the mirror.
Behind the mirror, at the position where the reflected light rays appear to diverge from.
Inside your own eye, where the light rays first crossed.

questions.question: A toy car is placed 15 cm in front of a flat vertical mirror. If the toy car is then moved 5 cm closer to the mirror, what is the new distance between the toy car and its virtual image?
options: 10 cm
20 cm
30 cm
40 cm

questions.question: You stand in front of a mirror and raise your right hand. Which of the following describes the image you see?
options: The image is upside down and appears to raise its left hand.
The image is the right way up and appears to raise its right hand on the same side.
The image is the right way up but appears to raise its left hand.
The image is upside down but appears to raise its right hand.

questions.question: A student places three different sheets of material in front of a flashlight: a sheet of clear glass, a sheet of frosted greaseproof paper, and a sheet of thick cardboard. Which statement correctly describes how they affect light?
options: The glass is opaque, the paper is transparent, and the cardboard is reflective.
The glass transmits light because it is transparent, while the cardboard does not transmit light because it is opaque.
The paper is transparent because it blocks all light, while the glass is opaque because it transmits light.
All three materials are transparent, but they transmit light at different speeds.

questions.question: A solid wooden ball is placed between a small lamp and a white screen. A dark shadow of the ball appears on the screen. Why does this shadow form?
options: The wooden ball bends the light rays around its edges, leaving a dark spot in the middle.
The wooden ball blocks the straight-travelling light rays, leaving an unlit area on the screen.
The wooden ball absorbs the darkness from the room and projects it onto the screen.
Light rays from the lamp slow down as they pass through the ball, creating a dim region.

questions.question: An oscilloscope displays two different sound waves. Wave A has a crest height (from the center line) of 2 cm, while Wave B has a crest height of 4 cm. Both waves have the same spacing between crests. How do these sounds compare?
options: Wave B has a higher pitch than Wave A, but they have the same volume.
Wave B is louder than Wave A, and they have the same pitch.
Wave A is louder than Wave B, and they have the same pitch.
Wave A has a higher pitch than Wave B, but they have the same volume.

questions.question: A guitar player tightens a string, causing it to vibrate much more rapidly (more times per second) when plucked. What change will a listener hear in the sound produced?
options: The sound will have a lower pitch because the frequency has increased.
The sound will have a higher pitch because the frequency has increased.
The sound will be much louder because the frequency has decreased.
The sound will be much quieter because the frequency has decreased.

questions.question: As you walk away from an outdoor concert speaker, the music becomes quieter. What is happening to the physical sound wave as it travels further through the air?
options: The frequency of the wave decreases, which makes the pitch sound lower.
The wave spreads out, causing the amplitude of the vibrations to decrease.
The wavelength of the sound decreases, causing the sound to travel faster.
The sound wave converts completely into light energy as it encounters air resistance.

questions.question: Why does sound travel significantly faster through an iron railway track than it does through the air?
options: Iron particles are completely hollow, allowing sound waves to pass through without any resistance.
The particles in iron are held by strong attractive forces, causing many particles to vibrate quickly when one does.
Iron particles do not vibrate at all, which allows sound to bypass them instantly.
Air particles have stronger attractive forces, which holds the sound wave back.

questions.question: An electric bell is placed inside a sealed glass jar. As an air pump removes all the air from the jar, the sound of the bell fades away until it cannot be heard, even though the hammer can still be seen striking the metal. Why does this happen?
options: The vacuum absorbs the light so we can see the hammer, but it blocks the sound from exiting the glass.
Sound waves require particles to vibrate and pass on the energy; without particles in a vacuum, sound cannot travel.
The lack of air pressure stops the metal bell from physically vibrating.
Sound travels so fast in a vacuum that it passes through the observer's ears without being detected.

questions.question: When a whistle is blown across a quiet room, a person on the other side hears it. What actually travels from the whistle to the person's ear?
options: Individual air particles from inside the whistle travel across the room and enter the person's ear.
A pattern of vibrations is passed from particle to particle, while the individual air particles only vibrate back and forth.
A stream of empty space is pushed through the air, carrying the sound energy.
Heat energy travels across the room, which the ear translates into sound.
